questions.stem: Which statement is a testable hypothesis for an investigation of yeast respiration?
options: Yeast is a type of fungus that is used to make bread rise and to brew beer
Yeast respiration is an interesting process that should be investigated further
Yeast might do something different when it is given more glucose to respire
If glucose concentration increases, the volume of CO₂ released by yeast in 10 minutes will increase
questions.explanation: A testable hypothesis predicts how a measurable dependent variable will respond to a change in the independent variable. A statement of fact about yeast makes no prediction, and a vague guess names nothing that can be measured.

questions.stem: Which question could be answered by a scientific investigation using primary data in a school laboratory?
options: Does the concentration of salt in water affect the germination rate of radish seeds?
Should the government fund more research into new drought-tolerant wheat varieties?
Is it morally acceptable to use animals to test new medicines for humans?
Which of the native birds in Australia is the most beautiful to look at?
questions.explanation: Salt concentration and germination rate can both be measured, so data collected by the student can answer the question. Funding, morality and beauty involve values and opinions that experiments cannot settle.

questions.stem: A student predicted that catalase activity would keep rising as temperature increased from 10°C to 70°C. Her data showed activity peaked at 40°C and then fell sharply. How should she modify her hypothesis?
options: Activity increases with temperature at every value tested, so the results above 40°C must be outliers
Activity decreases as temperature rises from 10°C, because heat always denatures enzyme molecules
Activity increases with temperature up to an optimum near 40°C, then decreases as the enzyme denatures
Activity is not affected by temperature, so the investigation should be repeated with a different enzyme
questions.explanation: A modified hypothesis should reflect the new evidence: a rise to an optimum followed by a fall. Discarding every result above 40°C as an outlier ignores a consistent pattern that the data clearly show.

questions.stem: Students soak potato strips in salt solutions of different concentrations and record the change in mass of each strip. What is the dependent variable?
options: The change in mass of each potato strip
The concentration of the salt solution
The length of time the strips are soaked
The type of potato used for every strip
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change the student makes, here the change in mass. Salt concentration is the independent variable, and soaking time and potato type are controlled variables.

questions.stem: In an investigation of the effect of pH on amylase, one tube contains starch and amylase that has been boiled. What is the purpose of this tube?
options: It is an experimental control, showing that starch is not broken down without active enzyme
It is a controlled variable, keeping the temperature of all the other tubes exactly the same
It is the independent variable, because it changes the pH of the solution in that tube
It is a repeat trial, used to show that the results of the other tubes are reliable
questions.explanation: An experimental control is set up so any change in the test tubes can be attributed to the active enzyme. A controlled variable is a factor held constant across all tubes, such as temperature, which is a different idea.

questions.stem: Students test whether light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed. The lamp is moved closer for each trial, but the water warms as the lamp gets closer. Which aspect of the investigation is most affected?
options: Validity, because temperature is also changing along with light intensity
Precision, because the bubbles produced cannot be counted to a decimal place
Reliability, because each light intensity was tested only once by the students
Accuracy, because the lamp was not calibrated against a light meter beforehand
questions.explanation: When a second variable changes along with the independent variable, the investigation no longer tests only the intended factor, so its validity suffers. A heat filter or a beaker of water between lamp and plant would control temperature.

questions.stem: How is reliable primary data obtained in an investigation?
options: By using the most expensive equipment that is available
By recording only results that support the hypothesis
By rounding every measurement to a whole number
By repeating trials and checking the results are consistent
questions.explanation: Reliability is about consistency: repeated trials that give similar results show the data can be trusted. Selecting only supporting results is a form of bias, not a way to improve reliability.

questions.stem: A student is researching the effects of a pesticide on native bees. Which source is likely to be the most reliable?
options: A blog post by a gardener describing what happened to the bees in her own backyard
A website run by the pesticide's manufacturer advertising the product
A social media video with many views claiming the pesticide kills all bees
A peer-reviewed journal article reporting a field study with stated methods
questions.explanation: Peer-reviewed research has been checked by independent experts and states its methods, so others can judge and repeat it. A manufacturer's website has a commercial interest, and anecdotes and viral videos are not systematic evidence.

questions.stem: In a risk assessment, what is the difference between a hazard and a risk?
options: A hazard is a minor injury; a risk is a serious injury that needs medical treatment
A hazard is something that could cause harm; a risk is the likelihood and severity of that harm
A hazard is the chance of harm occurring; a risk is the object or substance that causes it
A hazard applies only to chemicals; a risk applies only to equipment such as glassware
questions.explanation: A hazard is a potential source of harm, such as a sharp scalpel or a corrosive acid. Risk combines how likely harm is with how serious it would be, and control measures aim to reduce it.

questions.stem: Students will dissect a sheep's heart using scalpels. Which control measure best reduces the main risk?
options: Wash hands with soap after the lesson, because the heart may carry bacteria
Keep the heart in a refrigerator until it is used, so that it stays fresh
Cut away from the body on a dissecting board, with the heart held by forceps
Wear safety glasses at all times, because the heart may splash blood into the eyes
questions.explanation: The main hazard in this dissection is the sharp blade, so cutting away from the body on a stable board, holding tissue with forceps, reduces the chance of a cut. Hand washing manages a smaller, different risk and does not address the scalpel.

questions.stem: A student needs to add exactly 7.5 mL of enzyme solution to each test tube. Which piece of equipment is most appropriate?
options: A 100 mL measuring cylinder
A 50 mL conical flask
A 10 mL graduated pipette
A 250 mL glass beaker
questions.explanation: A graduated pipette with a capacity close to the volume needed gives the finest graduations and the most precise measurement. Beakers and flasks have only rough volume markings, and a 100 mL cylinder is too coarse for 7.5 mL.

questions.stem: Researchers plan an experiment on mice. Under the 3Rs principle used in Australia, which change shows 'reduction'?
options: Using a statistical design that gets valid results from fewer mice
Replacing the mice entirely with cultured human cells grown in dishes
Giving the mice pain relief and enriched cages during the study
Ending the study early whenever the mice start to show distress
questions.explanation: Reduction means using the smallest number of animals that will give valid results. Using cell cultures instead of animals is replacement, and pain relief and better housing are refinement.

questions.stem: When reading the volume of water in a measuring cylinder, how should the student avoid parallax error?
options: Read the volume from below the cylinder, looking up through the base
Read the volume twice from slightly different angles and average them
Read the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with the liquid surface
Read the top edge of the meniscus while looking down at it from directly above
questions.explanation: Parallax error occurs when the scale is viewed from an angle. Keeping the eye level with the bottom of the meniscus gives the correct reading; viewing from above makes the volume appear different from its true value.

questions.stem: Which table heading layout is best for recording results of an investigation into temperature and the rate of oxygen production?
options: First column 'Mean', then the trials, then 'Temperature' as the last column without units
A single column listing every reading in the order taken, with temperature noted beside each
First column 'Temperature (°C)', then columns 'Trial 1', 'Trial 2', 'Trial 3' and 'Mean' in 'mL/min'
First column 'Oxygen produced', second column 'Temperature', with units given in a note below
questions.explanation: Results tables put the independent variable in the first column and the dependent variable, with repeats and a mean, in later columns. Units belong in the column headings, not beside each value or in a footnote.

questions.stem: Under a microscope, a cheek cell measures 0.055 mm across. What is this in micrometres?
options: 550 µm
55 µm
5.5 µm
questions.explanation: There are 1000 µm in 1 mm, so 0.055 mm × 1000 = 55 µm. Multiplying by 100 instead of 1000 gives 5.5 µm, a common conversion slip.

questions.stem: A leaf disc has an area of 1.2 cm². What is its area in mm²?
options: 12 mm²
1200 mm²
0.12 mm²
120 mm²
questions.explanation: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 cm² = 10 × 10 = 100 mm², and 1.2 cm² = 120 mm². Using a factor of 10 for an area forgets that both dimensions are converted.

questions.stem: Students count the number of plant species in four habitats: rainforest, woodland, heath and grassland. Which representation is most appropriate?
options: A pie chart, because each habitat is a part of the whole
A column graph, because habitat is a categorical variable
A line graph, because the habitats follow on from each other
A scatter graph with a line of best fit through the points
questions.explanation: Habitat types are categories with no numerical order, so a column (bar) graph is used. A line graph or scatter graph implies a continuous independent variable, and the species counts are not parts of one total.

questions.stem: What is a dichotomous key used for in biology?
options: Recording the abiotic factors measured at regular intervals along a transect
Identifying organisms through a series of paired choices about their features
Showing the evolutionary relationships between species and their common ancestors
Calculating the population size of a species from a sample of marked animals
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key leads the user through pairs of contrasting statements until the organism is identified. Evolutionary relationships are shown by phylogenetic trees, not keys.

questions.stem: A student copies a graph from a government website into her report. What must she do?
options: Redraw the graph in different colours so that it becomes her own original work and needs no credit
Mention the website in her conclusion only, because graphs do not need references in reports
Acknowledge the source beside the graph and list it in the reference list using an accepted style
Nothing, because information on a government website is free for anyone to use without credit
questions.explanation: Any data or image taken from another source must be acknowledged, in the text or caption and in a reference list, in a consistent style such as APA. Redrawing a graph still uses someone else's data.

questions.stem: Rates of photosynthesis were 4, 8, 12, 12 and 12 units at light intensities of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 units. Which description of the relationship is correct?
options: Rate increases exponentially, doubling with each increase of 10 units in light intensity
Rate is directly proportional to light intensity up to 30 units, then stays constant
Rate increases steadily with light intensity across the whole range that was tested
Rate is inversely proportional to light intensity, falling as the light gets brighter
questions.explanation: From 10 to 30 units, rate ÷ light intensity is 0.4 each time, so rate is directly proportional to intensity; above 30 units it plateaus, so another factor has become limiting. It does not double with each 10-unit step.

questions.stem: A mark-release-recapture study estimates a lizard population at 180. A complete count later finds 200 lizards. What is the percentage error of the estimate?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = (difference ÷ accepted value) × 100 = (20 ÷ 200) × 100 = 10%. Dividing by the estimate (20 ÷ 180) gives about 11%, but the accepted value is the true count.

questions.stem: Pulse rates of five students after exercise were 112, 98, 125, 104 and 131 beats per minute. What is the range?
options: 19 beats per minute
33 beats per minute
27 beats per minute
114 beats per minute
questions.explanation: Range = highest value − lowest value = 131 − 98 = 33 beats per minute. 114 is the mean of the five values, which is a measure of centre, not spread.

questions.stem: Five trials of the time for a starch solution to clear were 52 s, 49 s, 51 s, 88 s and 48 s. The 88 s trial was an obvious mistake. What is the mean after excluding the outlier?
questions.explanation: Without the outlier, (52 + 49 + 51 + 48) ÷ 4 = 200 ÷ 4 = 50 s. Including 88 s gives 57.6 s, a mean pulled upwards by one faulty result.

questions.stem: Germination times in days for eight seeds were 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7 and 9. The mean is 5 days. Using the population standard deviation (dividing by n), what is the standard deviation?
options: 4.0 days
7.0 days
2.5 days
2.0 days
questions.explanation: The squared deviations sum to 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 32, and 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so the standard deviation is √4 = 2.0 days. 4.0 is the variance before the square root is taken, and 7 is the range.

questions.stem: Two groups measured the same leaf length. Group A's mean was 6.2 cm with a standard deviation of 0.1 cm; group B's mean was 6.2 cm with a standard deviation of 0.6 cm. What can be concluded?
options: Group A's measurements were more accurate, because a smaller standard deviation means a truer value
Group B's measurements were more reliable, because a larger standard deviation shows more data
The two groups were equally precise, because they recorded exactly the same mean leaf length
Group A's measurements were more precise, because they were spread less around the mean
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures spread, so a smaller value shows readings clustered closely together, which is precision. It says nothing about how close the mean is to the true length, which is accuracy.

questions.stem: What does it mean for a measurement to be accurate?
options: It was made with a digital instrument
It is close to the true or accepted value
It agrees closely with repeated measurements
It is recorded to many decimal places
questions.explanation: Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Agreement between repeated readings is precision, and many decimal places or a digital display do not guarantee either.

questions.stem: A pH probe is placed in a buffer solution known to be pH 7.00. Its readings are 7.41, 7.40 and 7.42. Which evaluation and fix is correct?
options: Accurate and precise, because the three readings differ from each other by only 0.02
Inaccurate and imprecise, from a random error; replace the buffer with distilled water
Precise but inaccurate, from a systematic error; calibrate the probe with standard buffers
Accurate but imprecise, from a random error; take many more readings and average them
questions.explanation: The readings agree closely (precise) but are all about 0.4 too high (inaccurate), which is the signature of a systematic error. Averaging more readings reduces random error but cannot remove a constant offset; calibration can.

questions.stem: Students measure water loss from a leafy shoot using a potometer. Which change would most improve the validity of comparing water loss in still air and moving air?
options: Record the position of the air bubble to more decimal places using a finer scale
Repeat the moving-air trial five times but keep only one trial in still air
Calculate a percentage error by comparing the result with a textbook value
Use the same shoot, or shoots of equal leaf area, at the same temperature and light for both conditions
questions.explanation: A valid comparison changes only the independent variable, air movement, so leaf area, temperature and light must be controlled. A finer scale improves precision and uneven repeats affect reliability, not validity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes reliability from validity?
options: Reliable results have no errors at all; valid results have only small random errors in measurement
Reliable results are consistent when repeated; valid results come from a test that measures what it intends to
Reliable results are close to the true value; valid results agree closely with each other when repeated
Reliable results come from a fair test; valid results are those that support the original hypothesis
questions.explanation: Reliability is about consistency across repeats; validity is about whether the method tests what it claims to, with other variables controlled. Closeness to the true value is accuracy, a third idea.

questions.stem: On a graph of enzyme activity against substrate concentration, all points lie on a smooth curve except one, which sits well below it. The student checks her notes and finds that tube was left standing for longer before testing. What should she do?
options: Identify it as an outlier, give the reason, leave it out of the line of best fit and repeat that trial
Draw the curve through every point, including this one, so that no data are hidden from the reader
Delete the point from her results table without comment, because it does not match the other values
Change the value to match the curve, because the trend shows what the true result should have been
questions.explanation: An outlier with a known cause should be identified, explained and excluded from the trend, and the trial repeated if possible. Deleting it without comment or altering the value misrepresents the data.

questions.stem: A student's data on yeast respiration cover temperatures from 10°C to 40°C. She uses the trend to predict the rate at 70°C. Why is this prediction unreliable?
options: It is an extrapolation beyond the tested range, where the relationship may change
It is an interpolation, which can only be made from data with no random errors
Predictions can never be made from a graph of results from a biological investigation
The prediction would be accurate only if the rate were recorded at more temperatures below 10°C
questions.explanation: Extending a trend beyond the measured range assumes the relationship continues, but enzymes in yeast denature at high temperatures, so the trend breaks down. Interpolation within the tested range is far more trustworthy.

questions.stem: In a survey of 12 students, those who slept more scored higher on a memory test. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Students with good memories need more sleep, so memory ability determines how long people sleep
Sleep and memory scores are positively correlated in this small sample, but cause is not shown
Sleeping more causes better memory, so all students should sleep at least nine hours a night
Memory scores have no relationship with sleep, because the sample contained only 12 students
questions.explanation: A survey shows an association, not a cause, and a sample of 12 is too small to generalise. Claiming sleep causes better memory, or the reverse, goes beyond what the data can support.

questions.stem: A student judges when iodine stops turning blue-black in starch tests by eye, and her repeat times vary widely. Which improvement would best address this limitation?
options: Ask several classmates to judge the colour as well and record the fastest time
Use a colorimeter to measure the colour change against a fixed endpoint reading
Use a larger beaker so that the colour of the mixture is easier for her to see clearly
Record the times to more decimal places using a stopwatch accurate to 0.01 s
questions.explanation: Judging colour by eye is subjective, which causes random variation; a colorimeter gives an objective reading. Timing to 0.01 s adds false precision when the endpoint itself is uncertain.

questions.stem: A bacterial population doubles every 20 minutes in ideal conditions. Starting with 100 cells, how many cells does a simple mathematical model predict after 2 hours?
options: 1200 cells
600 cells
3200 cells
6400 cells
questions.explanation: Two hours is 120 ÷ 20 = 6 doublings, so 100 × 2⁶ = 100 × 64 = 6400 cells. Multiplying 100 by 6 treats the growth as additive rather than doubling.

questions.stem: A class models the cell membrane with a layer of soap film and floating plastic beads. What is the main reason scientists use models like this?
options: To replace experiments, because a model proves an idea without any need for further evidence
To make the membrane look more interesting, because the real membrane has no definite structure
To represent a structure too small to see directly, while accepting it simplifies the real thing
To show the exact structure of the membrane, with every molecule shown at its correct size
questions.explanation: Models make invisible or complex structures easier to understand and test, but every model leaves things out. A model supports explanation and prediction; it does not prove an idea or show every detail exactly.

questions.stem: Why is scientific knowledge described as both contestable and testable?
options: Scientists vote on which ideas to accept, and the result can change after every new election held
Once an idea has been tested in one experiment it becomes a law and can no longer be challenged
Scientific ideas are opinions, so any idea is as valid as another whatever the evidence shows
Claims can be challenged and checked with new evidence, and revised if the evidence does not support them
questions.explanation: Scientific claims must make predictions that can be tested, and any claim can be questioned and replaced if better evidence appears. Acceptance rests on evidence, not voting or opinion, and no single experiment puts an idea beyond challenge.

questions.stem: A student finds that her enzyme results do not match a published study. Checking her method, she discovers the published study used a buffer to hold pH constant and she did not. What is the best response?
options: Repeat the investigation with a buffer added, since uncontrolled pH may explain the difference
Conclude that the published study is wrong, because her own results come from primary data
Report her results as they are, because a single method should never be changed once begun
Average her results with the published ones so the two sets of data come out the same
questions.explanation: New evidence about a likely uncontrolled variable is a reason to modify the investigation and test again. Averaging different studies' data, or assuming either study is wrong without testing, does not resolve the difference.

questions.stem: What is the role of peer review in science?
options: The author's friends check the spelling and formatting of the report before printing
The public votes on whether a study's conclusions should be accepted by scientists
A government department approves the results so that they become official policy
Independent experts evaluate a study's methods and conclusions before it is published
questions.explanation: In peer review, other scientists in the field scrutinise the methods, analysis and conclusions, which helps catch errors and unsupported claims. It is not a check of presentation, a public vote or government approval.

questions.stem: How should the scientific name of the mountain ash, Eucalyptus regnans, be written in a typed report?
options: In plain type, with the whole name in capital letters to make it stand out
In italics, with the species name first and the genus name second, both capitalised
In italics, with the genus capitalised and the species name in lower case
In bold, with both the genus and the species names starting with capitals
questions.explanation: Binomial names are italicised (underlined when handwritten), with the genus capitalised and the species name in lower case. The genus always comes first.

questions.stem: A student is presenting the results of a local water-quality study to a primary school class. Which approach best suits the audience and purpose?
options: Technical terms used without explanation, so that the science is not oversimplified
Simple language, a clear photo or diagram and one key finding, with terms explained
A full table of raw data with standard deviations and a detailed statistical analysis
The complete written report with a reference list read aloud word for word
questions.explanation: Scientific communication is matched to its audience: young students need plain language, visuals and a focused message. Raw data tables and statistics suit a scientific audience, not a primary class.
